text: Fox Broadcasting Company, LLC, stylized in all caps as FOX, is an American commercial broadcast television network and the flagship property of Fox Corporation, operated through Fox Entertainment. Launched by News Corporation on October 9, 1986, it emerged as a competitor to the Big Three networks—American Broadcasting Company (ABC), Columbia Broadcasting System (CBS), and National Broadcasting Company (NBC). Fox became the most successful attempt at a fourth television network, achieving the highest-rated free-to-air position in the 18–49 demographic from 2004 to 2012 and again from 2020 to 2021, and was the most-watched American television network in total viewership during the 2007–08 season. It is a member of the North American Broadcasters Association and the National Association of Broadcasters. Unlike other major networks, Fox does not operate its own news division and instead relies on Fox News, Fox Business Network, and Fox Weather for news programming. Fox and its affiliated companies operate entertainment channels internationally, though programming differs from the American network. In Canada, most viewers have access to at least one American-based Fox affiliate via over-the-air or pay television, but Fox's NFL broadcasts and most prime time programming are subject to simultaneous substitution rules imposed by the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) to protect domestic network rights. Fox is headquartered at 1211 Avenue of the Americas in Midtown Manhattan, New York City, with additional offices at the Fox Network Center in Los Angeles and the Fox Media Center in Tempe, Arizona. 20th Century Fox (now 20th Century Studios) began television production as early as 1948 under TCF Television Productions until 1958, producing syndicated programs. After the DuMont Television Network closed in August 1956 due to financial difficulties, the NTA Film Network was launched as a fourth network, with 20th Century Fox producing content for it, though the film network failed after a few years. 20th Century Fox continued producing content for the Big Three networks, including Perry Mason, Batman, and M*A*S*H. While running Paramount Pictures, Barry Diller attempted to create a fourth network with the Paramount Television Service in 1977, which was canceled before broadcasting. Diller later joined 20th Century Fox. In March 1985, News Corporation paid $255 million for a 50% interest in TCF Holdings, the parent of 20th Century Fox. In May 1985, News Corporation paid $2.55 billion to acquire six major U.S. independent stations—WNEW-TV in New York, WTTG in Washington, D.C., KTTV in Los Angeles, KRIV-TV in Houston, WFLD-TV in Chicago, and KRLD-TV in Dallas—from Metromedia. WCVB-TV in Boston was part of the original deal but was spun off to Hearst Broadcasting. Two years later, News Corporation acquired WXNE-TV in Boston and changed its call letters to WFXT. Radio personality Clarke Ingram suggested that Fox is a revival or linear descendant of DuMont, as Metromedia was formed from DuMont’s remaining stations, WNEW-TV and WTTG, and DuMont’s original operations in Manhattan became the Fox Television Center. In 1985, 20th Century Fox announced plans to form a fourth network using its studios and the Metromedia stations for production and distribution. Organizational plans were delayed until regulatory hurdles were cleared. In December 1985, Rupert Murdoch paid $325 million to acquire the remaining equity in TCF Holdings from Marvin Davis. The Metromedia station acquisition was approved by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in March 1986, with WNEW-TV and KRLD-TV changing call letters to WNYW and KDAF, respectively. These six stations, reaching 22% of U.S. households, formed the Fox Television Stations group. All original owned-and-operated stations (except KDAF, which was sold to Renaissance Broadcasting in 1995 and became a WB affiliate) remain part of Fox today. Fox initially affiliated with the top-rated independent station in each market, but in some cases, such as Denver, Phoenix, and St. Louis, it affiliated with a second-tier independent station when a more established one declined. Due to these factors, Fox was forced to affiliate with UHF stations in most markets, similar to DuMont’s experience. Barry Diller, then head of Fox Inc., is credited with creating the network, with the New York Times noting in October 1986 that his "current obsession" was creating a network to compete with NBC, CBS, and ABC. The network officially debuted with a soft launch at 11:00 p.m. Eastern and Pacific Time on Thursday, October 9, 1986, featuring a late-night talk show, The Late Show, hosted by Joan Rivers. The show quickly declined in ratings and was discontinued by early 1987 after Rivers and her husband Edgar Rosenberg left due to creative disagreements. The program then used guest hosts, and some affiliates, such as WCGV-TV in Milwaukee and WDRB-TV in Louisville, signed on under the condition they would not carry The Late Show. Before its April 5, 1987 launch, Fox rebranded from FBC to "Fox" under original President Garth Ancier, with ad man Jay Chiat suggesting the use of the "Fox" heritage and "searchlight" iconography to link the network to 20th Century Fox. Several station groups, including Media Central and Pappas Telecasting, initially avoided Fox but later joined. On April 5, 1987, Fox held its "grand opening" by expanding into prime time, premiering Married... with Children and The Tracey Ullman Show on Sunday nights. Both shows were rebroadcast at 7:00 and 7:30 p.m. Eastern/Pacific to allow viewers to sample programming without missing major network programs. Over the next several weeks, Fox added new shows, including 21 Jump Street, Mr. President, and Duet, completing its Sunday schedule. On July 11, 1987, the network launched its Saturday night lineup with the two-hour pilot of Werewolf, followed by The New Adventures of Beans Baxter, Karen's Song, and Down and Out in Beverly Hills, which were canceled by the start of the 1987–88 season and replaced by Second Chance and Women in Prison, both canceled by mid-1988. Fox had planned to cancel The Late Show and develop The Wilton North Report, but after a ratings resurgence under guest host Arsenio Hall, the network could not reach a deal with Hall to return as host and instead revived The Late Show in early 1988. The show then used guest hosts and eventually selected Ross Shafer as permanent host, only to be canceled by October 1988, while Hall signed a deal with Paramount Television to develop The Arsenio Hall Show. Fox aired the 39th Primetime Emmy Awards and the next five editions. Although Married... with Children and The Tracey Ullman Show had modest success, several affiliates, including KMSP-TV in Minneapolis and KPTV in Portland, Oregon, disaffiliated in 1988 due to weak programming, citing that the network’s offerings harmed their syndicated programming. At the start of the 1989–90 season, Fox added a third night of programming on Mondays. The season marked a turnaround, with the debut of The Simpsons, an animated series that originated as shorts on The Tracey Ullman Show. Ranked a three-way tie for 29th in the Nielsen ratings, it became a breakout hit and the first Fox series to break into the Top 30. As of 2025, The Simpsons is the longest-running American sitcom, the longest-running American animated program, and the longest-running American scripted primetime television series. In 1989, Fox introduced the documentary series Cops and the crime-focused magazine program America's Most Wanted, which debuted as a half-hour series on Sundays before expanding to an hour and moving to Fridays in the 1990–91 season. These series became staples on the network for over two decades and formed the nucleus of Fox’s Saturday night schedule starting in the 1994–95 season. Married... with Children, which centered on a dysfunctional lower-middle-class family, saw a significant increase in viewer interest after Michigan homemaker Terry Rakolta began a boycott in 1989 over risqué humor and sexual content. The show became Fox’s longest-running live-action sitcom, airing for 11 seasons. Fox survived where DuMont and other fourth-network attempts had failed because it operated just under the FCC’s legal threshold for a network, allowing it to generate revenue without adhering to the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules that applied to the Big Three. DuMont faced regulatory barriers, including a ban on acquiring additional stations and tighter FCC ownership limits, which restricted its growth. In contrast, Murdoch was willing to invest heavily in programming and talent. DuMont operated on a shoestring budget and could not retain programs or stars. Most later startup networks, such as UPN and The WB, followed Fox’s model. DuMont operated during a time when the FCC did not require television manufacturers to include UHF capability, so viewers had to buy expensive converters to access UHF stations, which had poor signal quality compared to VHF stations. By the time Fox launched, cable allowed UHF stations to compete equally with VHF stations. Fox was not initially considered a major competitor to the Big Three, as it targeted a younger demographic—adults aged 18 to 34—with edgier content, while the Big Three focused on older audiences. Until the early 1990s, most Fox stations were formatted as independent stations, airing first-run or acquired programming, and during prime time, either syndicated shows or movies. Few stations carried local newscasts, especially in early years, with only a few in larger markets retaining long-standing newscasts, and those were limited to one newscast per day. On September 6, 1990, Fox reached an agreement with TCI, the nation’s largest cable company, to establish a cable-only national feed, Foxnet, for markets without over-the-air affiliates. Foxnet launched on June 6, 1991, bringing Fox programming to smaller markets and reaching 1.3 million subscribers by 1992. As Fox expanded its prime time offerings to Thursday and Friday nights in the 1990–91 season, it scheduled The Simpsons against NBC’s The Cosby Show, and later introduced Beverly Hills, 90210, which became the network’s longest-running drama, airing for ten seasons. The show performed well in its Thursday slot, spending four seasons there and helping launch Martin, a Fox comedy that became a hit when it debuted in August 1992. The Simpsons returned to Sunday nights in the fall of 1994 and has remained there since. In Living Color, which debuted in April 1990, created memorable characters and launched the careers of Jim Carrey, Jamie Foxx, Damon Wayans, Marlon Wayans, Keenen Ivory Wayans, Chris Rock, Tim Meadows, Rosie Perez, and Jennifer Lopez. The show gained international prominence when Fox aired a live special during Super Bowl XXVI in January 1992, replacing CBS’s halftime show, marking the start of Fox’s rivalry with the Big Three and popularizing counterprogramming. The early and mid-1990s saw the debuts of several soap opera-style prime time dramas aimed at younger audiences, including Beverly Hills, 90210, Melrose Place (which initially had mediocre ratings but saw a significant viewership increase after Heather Locklear joined), the short-lived spin-off Models Inc., and the family drama Party of Five.

A television network that debuted in April 1990 created many memorable characters and launched the careers of future movie stars Jim Carrey, Jamie Foxx, Damon Wayans, Marlon Wayans, Keenen Ivory Wayans, guest stars Chris Rock and Tim Meadows, and both members of the show's dance troupe, the "Fly Girls," Rosie Perez and Jennifer Lopez. The series gained international prominence after Fox aired a special live episode in January 1992 as an alternative to the halftime show during Super Bowl XXVI, which was broadcast on CBS, marking the start of Fox's rivalry with the "Big Three" networks while popularizing the counterprogramming strategy against the Super Bowl telecast. During the early and mid-1990s, several soap opera-style prime time dramas aimed at younger audiences debuted and became quick hits, including Beverly Hills, 90210, its adult-focused spin-off Melrose Place (which initially had a mediocre ratings performance, before viewership rose significantly midway through its first season following Heather Locklear's addition to the cast), its short-lived spin-off Models Inc., and family drama Party of Five. The network also launched several series aimed at a black audience, including Martin, Living Single, and police procedural New York Undercover. Despite having a few successful shows like the science fiction drama The X-Files, Fox still lacked credibility among viewers, with many in the television industry viewing it as "the one that has that cartoon show" (The Simpsons), and more than 85% of affiliates in 1993 were UHF stations. Fox became a viable competitor to the older networks when it won broadcast television rights to the National Football League (NFL) away from CBS. In December 1993, Fox signed a contract with the NFL to televise games from the National Football Conference (NFC)—which had been airing its games on CBS since 1956—starting with the 1994 season. The initial four-year contract, which Fox bid $1.58 billion to obtain—while CBS offered $295 million per year to retain the rights—also included the exclusive U.S. television rights to Super Bowl XXXI in 1997. The network lured Pat Summerall, John Madden, Dick Stockton, Matt Millen, James Brown, Terry Bradshaw, and behind-the-scenes production personnel from CBS Sports to staff its NFL coverage. Shortly afterward, News Corporation began striking affiliation deals with, and later purchasing, more television station groups. On May 23, 1994, Fox agreed to purchase a 20% stake in New World Communications, a television and film production company controlled by investor Ronald Perelman that had recently entered broadcasting through its 1993 purchase of seven stations owned by SCI Television. As a result of Fox acquiring a 20% minority interest in the company, New World signed an agreement to switch the affiliations of twelve stations (eight CBS affiliates, three ABC affiliates [two of which were subsequently placed in a blind trust and then sold directly to Fox due to conflicts with FCC ownership rules], and one NBC affiliate) that it had either already owned outright or was in the process of acquiring from Citicasters and Argyle Communications to Fox starting in September 1994 and continuing as existing affiliation contracts with their existing major network partners expired. That summer, SF Broadcasting, a joint venture between Fox and Savoy Pictures founded in March 1994, purchased four stations from Burnham Broadcasting (three NBC affiliates and one ABC affiliate); through a separate agreement, those stations would also switch to Fox between September 1995 and January 1996 as existing affiliation agreements lapsed. These two deals were not the first instances in which a longtime "Big Three" station affiliated with Fox: in Miami, the affiliation moved from WCIX (channel 6) to NBC affiliate WSVN in January 1989 as the result of a complicated six-station affiliation swap in two South Florida markets spurred by NBC's purchase of CBS affiliate WTVJ (channel 4) and CBS's purchase of WCIX. WSVN immediately attracted industry notice for featuring a news-intensive tabloid format uncharacteristic of any Fox affiliate or independent station, with then-Fox network president Lucie Salhany calling WSVN "the future of television" in May 1994. WSVN remains the largest Fox affiliate in terms of market size to have entirely eschewed any prominent on-air branding with the network name. The NFC contract was the impetus for the affiliation deal with New World and SF Broadcasting's purchase of the Burnham stations, as Fox sought to improve local coverage of its new NFL package by aligning the network with stations that had more established histories and advertiser value than its charter affiliates. The deals spurred a series of affiliation realignments between all four U.S. television networks involving individual stations and various broadcasting groups such as those between CBS and Group W (whose corporate parent later bought the network in August 1995), and ABC and the E. W. Scripps Company (which owned three Fox affiliates that switched to either ABC or NBC as a result of the New World deal), affecting 30 television markets between September 1994 and September 1996. The two deals also had the side benefit of increasing local news programming on the new Fox affiliates, mirroring the programming format adopted by WSVN upon that station's switch to the network (as well as expanding the number of news-producing stations in Fox's portfolio beyond mainly charter stations in certain large and mid-sized markets). Fox Television Stations acquired New World outright on July 17, 1996, in a $2.48 billion stock purchase, making the latter's twelve Fox affiliates owned-and-operated stations of the network; the deal was completed on January 22, 1997. Later, in August 2000, Fox bought several stations owned by Chris-Craft Industries and its subsidiaries BHC Communications and United Television for $5.5 billion (most of these stations were UPN affiliates, although its Minneapolis station KMSP-TV would rejoin Fox in September 2002 as an owned-and-operated station). These purchases, for a time, made Fox Television Stations the largest owner of television stations in the U.S. (a title that has since been assumed by the Sinclair Broadcast Group, one of the network's largest affiliate groups). Fox completed its prime time expansion to all seven nights on January 19, 1993, with the launch of two additional nights of programming on Tuesdays and Wednesdays (the method of gradually adding nights to the programming schedule that began with the network's April 1987 prime time launch was replicated by The WB and UPN when those networks debuted in January 1995), making it the fifth broadcast network (behind the Dumont network) to air programming on a nightly basis. September 1993 saw the heavy promotion and debut of a short-lived western series that incorporated science-fiction elements, The Adventures of Brisco County, Jr. However, it was the supernatural investigative drama that debuted immediately following it on Friday nights, The X-Files, that would find long-lasting success, and would become Fox's first series to crack Nielsen's year-end Top 20 most-watched network programs. After several other failed attempts at late night programming following the cancellation of The Late Show (most notably, the quick failure of The Chevy Chase Show in 1993), Fox finally found success in that time period with the debut of MADtv on October 14, 1995; the sketch comedy series became a solid competitor to NBC's Saturday Night Live for over a decade and was Fox's most successful late night program as well as one of its most successful Saturday night shows, running for 14 seasons until 2009. An attempt to make a larger effort to program Saturday nights by moving Married... with Children from its longtime Sunday slot and adding a new but short-lived sitcom (Love and Marriage) to the night at the beginning of the 1996–97 season backfired with the public, as it resulted in a brief cancellation of America's Most Wanted that was criticized by law enforcement and public officials and was roundly rejected by viewers, which brought swift cancellation to the newer series. Married... quickly returned to Sundays (before moving again to Mondays two months later); both it and Martin would end their runs at the end of that season. The Saturday schedule was revised in November 1996, to feature one new and one encore episode of Cops, and the revived America's Most Wanted: America Fights Back. Cops and AMW remained the anchors of Fox's Saturday lineup, making it the most stable night in American broadcast television for over 14 years; both shows eventually were among the few first-run programs remaining on Saturday evenings across the four major networks after decreasing prime time viewership— as more people opted to engage in leisure activities away from home rather than watch television on that night of the week—led ABC, NBC and CBS to largely abandon first-run series on Saturdays (outside newsmagazines, sports and burned off prime time shows that failed on other nights) in favor of reruns and movies by the mid-2000s. America's Most Wanted ended its 22-year run on Fox in June 2011, and was subsequently picked up by Lifetime (before being cancelled for good in 2013); Cops, in turn, would move its first-run episodes to Spike in 2013 after 23 seasons (ending its original run on Fox as the network's longest-running prime time program), leaving sports and repeats of reality and drama series as the only programs airing on Fox on Saturday evenings. During the 1997–98 season, Fox had three shows in the Nielsen Top 20 (in terms of total viewers); The X-Files (which ranked 11th), King of the Hill (which ranked 15th) and The Simpsons (which ranked 18th), all of which aired on Sunday nights. Building around its flagship animated comedy The Simpsons, Fox would experience relative success with animated sitcoms in prime time, beginning with the debut of the Mike Judge-produced King of the Hill in 1997. Family Guy (the first of three adult-oriented animated series from Seth MacFarlane to air on the network) and Futurama (from Simpsons creator Matt Groening) would make their debuts in 1999; however, they were canceled in 2002 and 2003 respectively. Due to strong DVD sales and highly rated cable reruns on Cartoon Network's Adult Swim, Fox later decided to order new episodes of Family Guy, which began airing in 2005. Futurama would be revived with four direct-to-DVD films between 2007 and 2009 and would return as a first-run series on Comedy Central, where it ran from 2010 to 2013. Less successful efforts included The Critic, starring Saturday Night Live alumnus Jon Lovitz (which Fox picked up in 1994 after it was cancelled by ABC, only for the series to be cancelled again after its second season), and The PJs (which moved to The WB in 2000, after Fox cancelled that series after its second season). Other notable shows that debuted in the late 1990s included the quirky David E. Kelley-produced live-action dramedy Ally McBeal, the short-lived game show Greed, and the period comedy That '70s Show, the latter of which became Fox's second-longest-running live-action sitcom, airing for eight seasons. Throughout the 1990s and into the next decade, Fox launched a slate of cable channels beginning with the 1994 debuts of general entertainment network FX and movie channel FXM: Movies from Fox (now FX Movie Channel), followed by the debut of Fox News Channel in August 1996. Its sports operations expanded with the acquisition of controlling interests in several regional sports networks (including the Prime Network and SportsChannel) between 1996 and 2000 to form Fox Sports Net (which launched in November 1996), its 2000 purchase of Speedvision (later Speed Channel, which was replaced in the United States by Fox Sports 1 in August 2013; however, it continues to exist in other North American and Caribbean countries as Fox Sports Racing), and the launches of Fox Sports World (later Fox Soccer, which was replaced by FXX in September 2013) and Fox Sports en Español (now Fox Deportes) in the early 2000s. By 2000, many staple Fox shows of the 1990s had ended their runs. During the late 1990s and carrying over into the early 2000s, Fox put much of its efforts into producing reality shows many of which were considered to be sensationalistic and controversial in nature—such as Who Wants to Marry a Multi-Millionaire?, Temptation Island, Married by America, and Joe Millionaire (which became the first Fox program to crack the Nielsen Top 10), as well as video clip shows such as World's Wildest Police Videos and When Animals Attack!. After shedding most of these programs, Fox gradually filled its lineup with acclaimed dramas such as 24, The O.C., House, and Bones, and comedies such as The Bernie Mac Show, Malcolm in the Middle, and Arrested Development. As the decade wore on, Fox began surpassing ABC and NBC in the ratings, first in age demographics, then in overall viewership, and placed second behind a resurgent CBS in total viewership, beginning in 2002. Fox hit a major milestone in 2005 when it emerged as the most-watched U.S. broadcast network in the lucrative 18–49 demographic for the first time, largely boosted by the strength of the reality singing competition series American Idol. Regarded as the single most dominant program on 21st-century U.S. television, as well as the first Fox show to lead the Nielsen seasonal ratings, American Idol had peak audiences of up to 38 million viewers during the 2003 season finale and double-season average audiences of around 31 million viewers in 2006 and 2007. Subsequently, it leapfrogged over Fox's Big Three competition to become the highest-rated U.S. television program overall starting with the 2003–04 season, becoming the first reality singing competition series in the country to reach first place in the seasonal ratings. American Idol remains the most recent American television program to date to lead the national prime time ratings and attract at least 30 million viewers for multiple and consecutive television seasons. It is the most-watched program on American television by seasonal average viewership in the 2000s decade, as well as the most recent program scheduled to have successfully established a graveyard slot on American television since the end of NBC's Friends in 2004 and the subsequent decline of NBC's previously dominant "Must See TV" Thursday timeblock. By 2005, reality television succeeded sitcoms as the most popular form of entertainment in the United States as a result of Fox's rise with American Idol and NBC's network declines. House, which aired as American Idol's lead-out program on Tuesday nights, earned international prominence in the 21st century and became Fox's first prime time drama series (and the network's third program overall) to reach the Nielsen Top 10 beginning 2006. Beginning 2004, CBS and Fox, which ranked as the two most-watched broadcast networks in the U.S. during the 2000s, have tended to equal one another in demographic ratings among general viewership, with both networks winning certain demographics by narrow margins; however, while Fox has the youngest-skewing viewer base, CBS is consistently regarded to have the oldest audience demographics among the major broadcast networks. Fox hit a milestone in February 2005 by scoring its first sweeps victory in total viewership and demographic ratings, boosted largely by its broadcast of Super Bowl XXXIX and the strengths of American Idol, 24, House, and The O.C. In September 2006, as a result of the increasing number of over-the-air Fox affiliates and the increased availability of digital subchannels carrying Fox in certain markets, Foxnet was discontinued. Then, a sweeping milestone came by the conclusion of the 2007–08 season on May 21, 2008, shortly after the widely acclaimed seventh-season finale of American Idol, when Fox outranked longtime leader CBS as the most-watched television network overall in the United States, attributed to the strengths of Super Bowl XLII and its NFL game coverages, Idol and House during that season. To date, Fox is the only non-Big Three network to top the overall Nielsen ratings since its inception in the 1950–51 season. In the late 2000s, Fox launched a few series that proved to be powerful hits in different respects. In 2007, the network began production on the game shows Are You Smarter than a 5th Grader? and Don't Forget the Lyrics!; both shows ran for a total of three seasons each, making them the longest-running game shows in Fox's history. In 2008, the supernatural mystery series Fringe debuted to moderate ratings but earned critical acclaim during its first season on Tuesdays. Throughout its run, the series developed a large loyal fanbase that turned the show into a cult favorite. In 2009, Glee premiered to average ratings when its pilot aired as a lead-out program of the eighth-season finale of American Idol, but earned positive reviews from critics. The cast of the series has been acknowledged by Barack Obama and Oprah Winfrey, who have each asked the cast to perform live for various national events. At the beginning of the 2010s, new comedies Raising Hope and New Girl gave Fox its first live-action comedy successes in years. The second season of Glee delivered that series' highest ratings during the 2010–11 season, with viewership peaking during its Super Bowl lead-out episode in February 2011 (marking the most expensive post-Super Bowl episode ever produced on U.S. television). Fox has maintained several long-running game shows, making them the longest-running in the network’s history. The supernatural mystery series Fringe debuted in 2008 with moderate ratings but received critical acclaim during its first season on Tuesdays, eventually developing a large loyal fanbase that made it a cult favorite. Glee premiered in 2009 with average ratings when its pilot aired as a lead-out program for the eighth-season finale of American Idol, but earned positive reviews from critics. The show’s cast has been acknowledged by Barack Obama and Oprah Winfrey, who have each asked them to perform live at national events. In the early 2010s, Fox achieved its first live-action comedy successes in years with the new comedies Raising Hope and New Girl. The second season of Glee reached its highest ratings during the 2010–11 season, peaking during its Super Bowl XLV lead-out episode in February 2011, which was the most expensive post-Super Bowl episode ever produced on U.S. television. Glee consistently attracted worldwide media attention and built a large, loyal international fanbase. Fox’s live telecast of Super Bowl XLV in 2014 helped it become the first U.S. television network to earn an average single-night prime time audience of at least 100 million viewers. American Idol lost its position as the top-rated prime-time program during the 2011–12 finale, falling to second behind NBC Sunday Night Football, ending its eight-year streak as the top-rated prime-time broadcast network series in American television history, which included dominance in both the Adults 18–49 demographic and total viewership. Idol remained in the Nielsen Top 10 from 2003 to 2013 and was the highest-rated non-sports prime-time program and reality series in the U.S. from 2003 to 2012, marking the longest Nielsen ratings streaks for any Fox program in those categories. The 2012 season finale of American Idol marked the end of the 25th anniversary of the Fox network, during which it won the 18–49 demographic for the eighth consecutive season, the longest such streak according to Nielsen records (still standing as of 2026). However, Fox experienced a significant viewership decline during the 2012–13 season, with American Idol and Glee suffering steep ratings drops, and the network falling to third in total viewership (a 22% decrease) and second in the 18–49 demographic (a position it held as of 2014). This decline continued into the 2013–14 season, when Fox placed fourth among major networks in total viewership for the first time since 2001. On January 13, 2014, Fox announced it would abandon the traditional pilot season concept and instead directly pick up shows to series. The network achieved renewed ratings success with its February 2014 broadcast of Super Bowl XLVIII, which became the second most-watched television broadcast by average in U.S. history, and the lead-out programs New Girl and Brooklyn Nine-Nine. In May 2014, Kevin Reilly resigned as chairman of Fox Entertainment. On July 15, 2014, 21st Century Fox announced a merger of the network and 20th Century Fox Television into the newly created Fox Television Group, with Dana Walden and Gary Newman appointed as co-chairpersons. The 2014–15 season saw the series finale of Glee and the debut of new dramas Gotham and Empire. Empire’s ratings increased week-to-week throughout its first season, becoming the network’s first successful American Idol lead-out since House and the first American television program to consistently increase its episode-to-episode viewership during its first five weeks since ABC’s Roseanne in 1992. Empire ended its first season as the first American television show to increase its episodic viewership consistently throughout a single season and as Fox’s fourth program (and first since the 2013 finale of American Idol) to enter the Nielsen Top 10 by the end of the 2014–15 season. The 2015–16 season marked a notable turnaround for Fox, as it jumped ahead of ABC to third place in nationwide ratings (in both overall viewership and the 18–49 demographic) and achieved several firsts. This improvement was driven by the transfer of the Miss Universe and Miss USA pageants from NBC, as well as the return of The X-Files after its 2002 season end and the live musical special Grease: Live, which became the first live American television musical special of the 21st century to be broadcast in front of a live studio audience and the first live musical special aired by a non-Big Three network on primetime. By 2016, Empire and The X-Files ranked in the Nielsen Top 10 for the season, marking the first season since the 2007–2008 American Idol-House tandem that Fox had two programs in the Top 10 without American Idol or any other Fox reality show. The same year, American Idol concluded its original run on Fox after fifteen seasons, ending an era of one of the most successful shows in American television history. In February 2017, Fox broadcast Super Bowl LI, which attracted an average of 111.3 million viewers—ranking among the top five most-watched Super Bowl games and the second-highest audience in network history behind Super Bowl XLVIII. In March 2017, Rob Wade was named Fox’s new president of alternative entertainment and specials, having previously worked as a showrunner for Dancing with the Stars, head of entertainment for BBC Worldwide, and executive producer of America’s Got Talent and The X Factor. On July 27, 2018, 21st Century Fox shareholders agreed to sell most of its key assets—including 20th Century Fox and FX Networks—to The Walt Disney Company for $71.3 billion, following a spin-off of certain businesses. The sale did not include the Fox Broadcasting Company, television stations, or the Fox Sports, Fox News, and Fox Business cable channels, which were to be maintained under a new entity tentatively called "New Fox." Because Disney already owns ABC, the acquisition would have violated the FCC’s rules against merging any of the four major broadcast networks. As a result of the Disney/Fox deal and the December 4, 2019, merger of CBS and Viacom, Fox became the only major American broadcast network without a film studio. After the deal, Fox emphasized sports programming in its upfronts, including acquiring the NFL’s Thursday Night Football package and the rights to the FIFA World Cup. On June 27, 2018, WWE announced that SmackDown would move to Fox on Friday nights beginning October 4, 2019, under a five-year contract valued at $205 million per year. Fox also increased its non-scripted output, announcing The Masked Singer (based on the South Korean format King of Mask Singer), Mental Samurai, and Spin the Wheel for the 2018–19 season. In August 2018, Fox Television Group CEO Dana Walden stated the network planned to commission more series from independent studios not co-owned with the Big Three, citing limited opportunities due to vertical integration, and noted that top programs like The Big Bang Theory and This Is Us were distributed by third parties. Fox also planned to acquire new pitches directly from writers and offer them to outside producers, while gradually reducing scripted programming development from 20th Television, though The Simpsons would remain. Following the sale, Dana Walden became chairwoman of Disney Television Studios and ABC Entertainment. Charlie Collier succeeded Gary Newman as chairman and CEO of Fox on November 1, 2018, with Newman temporarily remaining in a transitional role. In early 2019, The Masked Singer premiered to Fox’s highest ratings for a non-scripted premiere without an NFL lead-in since 2011 and recorded the largest-ever Nielsen ratings gain for a non-scripted series after three days of delayed viewership. On January 30, 2019, Fox ordered a second season, with the first-season finale drawing an average audience of 11.5 million viewers. The next day, the "New Fox" entity, officially named Fox Corporation, began trading on March 19, 2019. At its 2019–20 upfronts, Fox announced 10 new scripted series, with three (Almost Family, Bless the Harts, and Prodigal Son) for the fall, and the second and third seasons of The Masked Singer scheduled for October 2019 and February 2020 (with the latter premiering after Super Bowl LIV). Fox also established Fox Alternative Entertainment, led by Rob Wade, for investments in non-scripted formats, with its first production being the second season of The Masked Singer. Thursday Night Football finished as the second highest-rated series of the 2018–19 season in the key demographic, behind only Sunday Night Football, while The Masked Singer tied for third with The Big Bang Theory and This Is Us. In the 2019–20 season, Thursday Night Football and The Masked Singer again finished as the second and third highest-rated programs in the key demographic, and Fox finished the season as the highest-rated network among viewers 18–49 (with CBS leading in overall viewers). Fox repeated this victory in the 2020–21 season but was narrowly beaten by NBC in the 2021–22 season by a tenth of a ratings share. In October 2022, Collier stepped down to join Roku, with Rob Wade promoted to president and CEO of Fox Entertainment. That season, Fox lost Thursday Night Football to Amazon Prime Video. In May 2023, Fox dropped its procedural drama 9-1-1 after six seasons, which had been the network’s scripted tentpole since 2018. As a 20th Television production, ABC picked up the series for a seventh season. Its spin-off, 9-1-1: Lone Star, remained on Fox and was renewed for a fifth season. In September 2024, it was announced that 9-1-1: Lone Star would conclude after its fifth season, becoming the last 20th Television-produced drama to air on the network. Fox also lost SmackDown to USA Network in September 2024, and began a strategy of regular sports programming on Friday nights, starting with a package of primetime college football games, leveraging its contract extension with the Big Ten Conference, which included options to carry Friday-night games after the addition of west coast teams. On April 2, 2025, Fox and 20th Television Animation announced a four-season, 15-episode renewal for The Simpsons, Bob’s Burgers, Family Guy, and American Dad!, marking the return of the latter to the network after an 11-year run on TBS from October 2014 to March 2025. As of 2015, Fox provides 17 hours of regularly scheduled network programming each week, including fifteen hours of prime time programming from Monday through Saturday (8:00 to 10:00 p.m. Eastern and Pacific) and Sunday (7:00 to 10:00 p.m.), and one hour of late night programming on Saturdays (11:00 p.m. to 12:00 a.m.), which is currently a repeat of primetime series. The network also airs a Sunday morning political discussion show, Fox News Sunday with Shannon Bream (9:00 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. Eastern and Pacific), its only regular national news program. Sports programming is typically aired on weekends, mostly between 11:00 a.m. and 11:30 p.m. ET, with the Saturday and Friday prime time blocks (starting in 2024) mainly scheduled for sports, and encores airing when no sports are scheduled. Except for The Critic, The PJs, and Futurama, which were cancelled in 1995, 2000, and 2003, Fox typically airs a Sunday night lineup of original adult animation sitcoms, all produced or co-produced by 20th Television. This block, known as Animation Domination from May 1, 2005, to September 14, 2014, was rebranded as Sunday Funday in 2014 after the reintroduction of live-action comedy series, though animated series remain a key part of the schedule. The first shows in the Animation Domination lineup were American Dad! (which moved to TBS in October 2014 and returned in early 2026), Family Guy (which returned after a three-year cancellation), The Simpsons (the longest-running cartoon on Fox, predating the lineup by 16 years), and King of the Hill (which predated the lineup by eight years). After King of the Hill’s cancellation, Family Guy’s spinoff The Cleveland Show aired from 2009 to 2013, and Bob’s Burgers began in 2011. Current animated shows in the lineup include The Simpsons, Family Guy, Bob’s Burgers, Krapopolis, Grimsburg, Universal Basic Guys, and American Dad! returning in early 2026. Other shows include Sit Down, Shut Up, Allen Gregory, Napoleon Dynamite, Bordertown, Bless the Harts, Duncanville, The Great North, Housebroken, and the live-action/animated hybrid Son of Zorn. An extension called Animation Domination High-Def launched on Saturday late nights in July 2013, marking the return of first-run programming in that slot since the 2010 cancellation of The Wanda Sykes Show. Due to low ratings, Fox announced on April 17, 2014, that it would discontinue the block, with the planned end on June 28, 2014, though it continued airing in encore form until the start of the 2016–17 season, when the hour returned to encores of comedies or reality series.

Fox will return in early-2026 with original episodes of American Dad!, Grimsburg, Opopolis, and Universal Basic Guys after over a decade of airing on TBS, alongside other shows such as Sit Down, Shut Up, Allen Gregory, Napoleon Dynamite, Bordertown, Bless the Harts, Duncanville, The Great North, Housebroken, and the live-action/animated hybrid Son of Zorn. In July 2013, an extension of the Sunday prime-time block called "Animation Domination High-Def" launched on Saturday late nights, marking the return of first-run programming in that slot since the 2010 cancellation of The Wanda Sykes Show; however, due to low ratings, Fox announced on April 17, 2014, that it would discontinue the block, which was scheduled to end on June 28, 2014, though it continued airing in encore form until the start of the 2016–17 season when the hour reverted to encores of comedies or reality series. Fox began airing children's programming on September 8, 1990, with the Fox Children's Network, which was rebranded as Fox Kids Network in 1991 and simply Fox Kids in 1998, airing on Saturday mornings and weekday afternoons; the block featured animated series such as Bobby's World, Eek! The Cat, X-Men, Spider-Man, The Tick, Fun House, Goosebumps, Casper, Dragon Ball Z (Ocean English dub), and Digimon, as well as live-action series and select Warner Bros. Animation shows like Tiny Toon Adventures, Animaniacs, and Batman: The Animated Series (which were moved to Kids' WB in September 1995); Mighty Morphin Power Rangers, from Saban Entertainment, was the block's most successful series, debuting in 1993 and serving as its flagship until it moved to ABC and Toon Disney in 2002. In October 2001, Fox sold its children's division, including Saban Entertainment and Fox Family Worldwide, to The Walt Disney Company for $5.3 billion; in January 2002, the Fox Kids block was reduced to Saturdays, with weekday hours turned over to affiliates; on September 14, 2002, it was replaced by FoxBox, later renamed 4Kids TV in January 2005, which aired programs such as Yu-Gi-Oh!, Kirby: Right Back at Ya!, Sonic X, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (2003), Shaman King, and One Piece. Fox discontinued 4Kids TV on December 27, 2008, due to disputes over unpaid lease fees and failure to guarantee station carriage, citing stiff competition from cable channels as a reason for ending children's programming; the network turned two of the four Saturday morning hours over to affiliates for local newscasts or educational content, while retaining two hours for Weekend Marketplace, which debuted on January 3, 2009. On September 13, 2014, Xploration Station, a two-hour syndicated block produced by Steve Rotfeld Productions that complies with the Children's Television Act and focuses on STEM fields, began airing on Fox stations owned by affiliate groups including Fox Television Stations and Tribune Broadcasting; stations may choose to carry Xploration Station, continue with Weekend Marketplace (as Sinclair Broadcast Group did, though it added the block to most affiliates in September 2016), or not carry it at all (as Gray Television did in Birmingham due to existing E/I contracts). Unlike ABC, CBS, and NBC, Fox does not air national news programs—morning, evening, or overnight—focusing instead on prime time, sports, and ancillary programming; although Fox Corporation owns Fox News Channel, which launched in October 1996 and has near-universal distribution via pay TV, it operates as a separate entity under the Fox News Group. Fox does produce content for the broadcast network, including prime time news segments anchored by Bill Hemmer, especially during political events, and coverage of the State of the Union, presidential debates, national elections, and breaking news branded as a "Fox News Special Report," "Fox News Alert," or "Fox News Red Alert," with carriage varying by station and often limited to prime time; Fox also airs Fox News Sunday on Sunday mornings and rebroadcasts it later, and operates Fox NewsEdge, launched in 1996, which provides national and international news for local newscasts. Fox first attempted a national news program with The Reporters, a weekly newsmagazine from 1988 to 1990, which was cancelled due to low ratings; from 1987 to about 1996, it aired news capsules branded as Fox News Extra and later Fox News Updates; in 1993, it launched Front Page with hosts Ron Reagan and Josh Mankiewicz, which failed to capture a younger audience; in 1998, Fox Files, hosted by Catherine Crier and Jon Scott, lasted over a year before cancellation; its last newsmagazine attempt was The Pulse in 2002–03, hosted by Shepard Smith; on May 17, 2016, the network aired an interview special with Megyn Kelly, Megyn Kelly Presents. Fox attempted national morning programs, beginning with Fox After Breakfast (1996–1998), hosted by Tom Bergeron, Laurie Hibberd, and Vicki Lawrence, which aired at 9:00 a.m. to accommodate local newscasts; it originated as Breakfast Time on FX in 1994; in 2002, it launched Good Day Live, a syndicated, entertainment-focused version of Good Day L.A., which was cancelled in 2005; on January 22, 2007, Fox premiered The Morning Show with Mike and Juliet on owned-and-operated stations, hosted by Mike Jerrick and Juliet Huddy, with a lighter, entertainment-oriented format that shifted during major news events; it was syndicated in 2007 to stations affiliated with ABC, NBC, and CBS and cancelled in June 2009. Fox believed sports, particularly professional football, would drive growth, and in 1987, offered the NFL $13 million per game for Monday Night Football, but the NFL renewed with ABC; in 1993, Fox bid $1.58 billion for the National Football Conference, winning the rights and ending CBS's football coverage for the first time since 1955, which established Fox as a major network and led to affiliation deals with New World Communications; Fox also acquired rights to the NHL (1994–99), Major League Baseball (since 1996), and NASCAR (since 2001, initially with NBC and TNT); from 2007 to 2010, it aired the Bowl Championship Series and the BCS National Championship Game (excluding Rose Bowl events); after the deal ended, it acquired rights to the Big Ten and Pac-12 football championship games (alternating yearly with ESPN); in 2017, Fox secured tier 1 rights to the Big Ten Conference. In August 2011, Fox and the UFC reached a multi-year agreement to broadcast four live events annually in prime time or late night, with the first event, Velasquez vs. Dos Santos, airing on November 12, 2011; the deal ended in 2018, with UFC events moving to ESPN and ESPN+. Fox's 2023 telecast of Super Bowl LVII remains the highest-rated U.S. television program on average in history, while its 2017 telecast of Super Bowl LI holds the record for the largest overall audience in U.S. television history. On June 13, 2024, Fox announced a multi-year deal to be the sole broadcaster of the IndyCar Series and its subsidiary Indy NXT. Fox has 18 owned-and-operated stations and affiliation agreements with 226 additional stations across 50 states, the District of Columbia, and three U.S. possessions; through Fox Television Stations, it has the most owned-and-operated stations among major American commercial networks. The network reaches 95.77% of U.S. households (299,268,292 Americans with at least one TV set); New Hampshire, New Jersey, and Delaware are the only states without a locally licensed Fox affiliate (New Hampshire via WFXT, New Jersey split between WNYW and WTXF, Delaware via WTXF and WBOC-DT2). Fox largely discontinued analog broadcasts on June 12, 2009, as part of the digital transition; it maintains a few low-power affiliates, such as WYFX-LD in Youngstown, Ohio, and in some markets, these stations simulcast on subchannels of co-owned full-power stations; Fox also has numerous subchannel-only affiliations in markets outside the top 50 Nielsen-designated markets, with WSYX-DT3 in Columbus, Ohio (No. 34 by Nielsen) being the largest by market size. Nexstar Media Group is Fox's largest affiliate group by market and numerical reach, with 42 stations (including former O&Os spun off in 2008 to Local TV, later acquired by Tribune in 2013, and purchased by Nexstar in 2019); the Sinclair Broadcast Group is the second-largest operator of Fox stations, owning or providing services to 26 affiliated stations. Fox previously distributed programming to underserved markets via Foxnet, a cable channel launched in 1991 and shut down on September 12, 2006, which aired syndicated and brokered programming; the concept influenced The WB 100+ Station Group (launched September 1998) and The CW Plus (launched September 2006), which allow localized branding and local advertising sales. Fox's programming schedule differs from the "Big Three" networks by airing only two hours of prime time programming on Monday through Saturday evenings and three hours on Sundays, compared to three hours on weekdays and four hours on Sundays for ABC, CBS, and NBC; this is referred to as "common prime," with the 10:00 p.m. (Eastern/Pacific)/9:00 p.m. (Central/Mountain) hour programmed only by the Big Three. Fox traditionally avoids programming the 10:00 p.m. hour, ceding it to local affiliates for newscasts, though exceptions exist for select special film presentations based on their running time.

Fox's prime time programming schedule differs from the "Big Three" networks (ABC, CBS, and NBC) by airing only two hours on Monday through Saturday evenings and three hours on Sundays, compared to the three hours from 8:00 to 11:00 p.m. on weekdays and four hours from 7:00 to 11:00 p.m. on Sundays (Eastern and Pacific Time) for the older networks. This schedule, known as "common prime," includes the 10:00 p.m. (Eastern/Pacific) or 9:00 p.m. (Central/Mountain) hour, which is programmed exclusively by ABC, CBS, and NBC. Fox traditionally avoids programming the 10:00 p.m. hour, allowing local affiliates to air local newscasts during that time, though exceptions occur for special film presentations that exceed a two-hour timeslot, live sports overruns, or primetime entertainment following NFL playoff games. Fox did schedule programming in the 10:00 p.m. hour on Sundays from September 1989 to September 1993, but never added programming at that hour on other nights. The original reason for the reduced prime time hours was to avoid FCC requirements that would have classified Fox as a network and imposed associated regulations, though these rules have since been relaxed. Unlike the "Big Three," Fox does not air national morning or evening newscasts or any network daytime programming (such as soap operas, game shows, or talk shows), and instead relies on its owned-and-operated stations and affiliates to produce or distribute syndicated daytime content, including programs like Divorce Court and The Wendy Williams Show, distributed by corporate sister 20th Television. Fox also does not carry children's programming on Saturday mornings or late-night programming on Monday through Friday nights, with local affiliates producing their own content or airing syndicated programs. Due to irregular sports scheduling, many Fox stations fill weekend afternoons with syndicated programming, infomercials, and movies. Fox produces two versions of program promotions: one with standard airtimes based on time zones and another with "clean" end tags allowing stations to insert local airtime and station information via graphical and verbal continuity. This practice, different from ABC, NBC, and CBS, which only allow station logo insertions, was later adopted by The WB, UPN, The CW, and MyNetworkTV. A third promo version is used for cable network advertising, featuring "check local listings" in the end tag. Fox is the only broadcast network that currently airs adult animated comedies, beginning with The Simpsons in 1989, followed by King of the Hill (1997, until 2009, with a return to Hulu in 2025), Family Guy (cancelled twice, revived by Adult Swim in reruns, returned by Fox in 2005 due to home video sales), Futurama (1999, until 2003, picked up by Adult Swim, then Comedy Central from 2008–2013, returned to Hulu in 2023), American Dad! (2005, until 2014, picked up by TBS until March 2025, returned the next year), The Cleveland Show (2009, until 2013), Bob's Burgers (2011), The Great North (2021, until 2025), Krapopolis (2023), and Grimsburg and Universal Basic Guys (2024). Other adult animated shows like The Critic, The PJs, Sit Down, Shut Up, Allen Gregory, Napoleon Dynamite, Bordertown, Son of Zorn (Fox's only live-action/animated hybrid sitcom), Bless the Harts, Duncanville, and Housebroken were short-lived and unsuccessful. While ABC, CBS, and NBC have attempted to replicate Fox's success with adult animated shows, none have succeeded. Within Fox's station group, locally produced news varies significantly compared to ABC, NBC, and CBS, which typically offer at least 4½ hours of local newscasts on weekdays and one hour on weekends. Most Fox stations run a late-evening newscast at 10:00 p.m. (Eastern/Pacific) or 9:00 p.m. (Central/Mountain), lasting 30 minutes to one hour, due to the network not programming that hour. Several charter stations, such as WNYW in New York City, which launched its 10:00 p.m. newscast in March 1967, already aired prime time newscasts before Fox's launch. Most Fox stations also offer a weekday morning newscast from 7:00 a.m., one to three hours long, as a local alternative to national morning news. Fox has fewer stations with independent news operations than the "Big Three"; as of October 2015, 70 of its 236 stations (including all 18 owned-and-operated stations) had in-house news departments, compared to roughly 5/8–7/8 of stations on the other networks. KVVU (channel 5) in Las Vegas has the highest weekly news programming hours among Fox stations at 78½ hours. Many Fox stations use a newscast-intensive schedule similar to ABC, NBC, or CBS affiliates, including midday or early-evening newscasts, often extended by half-hour to compete with national evening newscasts. Some stations, especially those not owned by Fox Television Stations or formerly owned by Tribune Broadcasting, air early-evening newscasts only Monday through Friday due to weekend sports overruns. WSVN in Miami was the first Fox station to adopt this format, moving its late newscast from 11:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. and expanding it to one hour in 1989, and increasing its weekday morning newscast by two hours. This format was later adopted by former major network stations that switched to Fox between 1994 and 1996. Many upstart news departments begin with only a prime time newscast before adding more over time. In smaller to mid-sized markets outside the top 50 Nielsen-designated markets, local Fox newscasts are often outsourced to NBC, ABC, or CBS affiliates due to lack of funds, studio space, or legal duopolies or management agreements. For example, WEMT (channel 39) in Greeneville, Tennessee, produces its newscasts via a local marketing agreement with WCYB-TV (channel 5), an NBC affiliate, owned by Sinclair Broadcast Group. Fox affiliates that outsource news often carry less programming than standalone stations, as the contracting affiliate avoids competition in common time slots, unlike same-market ABC, CBS, or NBC affiliates that may simulcast. Exceptions include KFOX-TV (channel 14) in El Paso and WXIN, which began producing newscasts for their CBS-affiliated duopoly partners in September 2014 and January 2015, respectively, maintaining their prior news programming levels. KNPN-LD (channel 26) in St. Joseph, Missouri, is the smallest Fox affiliate by market size with an in-house news operation since its July 2012 sign-on; after KNPG-LD (channel 21) and KCJO-LD (channel 30) joined NBC and CBS in November 2016 and June 2017, News-Press & Gazette Company expanded KNPN's production, though the station maintained roughly the same amount of programming. WPGH-TV (channel 53) in Pittsburgh, the largest Fox station by Nielsen market ranking (#23), outsources its news programming; WPXI (channel 11), an NBC affiliate, has produced its 10:00 p.m. newscast since 2006 after WPGH shut down its news department. The largest Fox station without news programming is WSYT (channel 68) in Syracuse, New York, which discontinued its 10:00 p.m. newscast in 2006. In Dayton, Ohio, Sinclair Broadcast Group adopted Fox 45 News as its universal brand in August 2015, even though the news department belongs to WKEF (ABC affiliate), due to WKEF's weaker ratings; in 2019, WRGT and WKEF switched to a 24/7 web news service called "Dayton 24/7 Now," and in 2021, Fox affiliation moved to WKEF's second subchannel as part of Sinclair's consolidation to address regulatory concerns. Fox offers video on demand through Fox on Demand, available on cable, satellite, streaming, and telecom providers, and streams programming on Hulu and via the Full Episode portal on Fox.com. The most recent episodes are typically available the day after broadcast on Fox on Demand, with fast forwarding disabled and original advertisements included for a week before being replaced by direct response ads. Due to a January 2012 policy to encourage live or same-week DVR viewing, Hulu and Fox.com impose an eight-day delay for most viewers, restricting day-after-air access to subscribers of certain pay providers (such as Dish Network and Verizon FiOS) or Hulu's free service with Yahoo! Stream; however, Hulu offers newer episodes to paid subscribers with a user login. In March 2020, Fox began streaming the full schedule of its owned stations through Fox Now. In April 2020, Fox acquired the ad-supported streaming service Tubi, which initially offered third-party licensed content but later began adding episodes of Fox original series a week after television premiere. Fox discontinued the Fox Now app in July 2023, with streaming continuing on Hulu, Fox Local, or Tubi; the service was effectively relaunched as Fox One two years later. Fox began broadcasting in 720p high definition on September 12, 2004, during the first week of the 2004 NFL season. Until March 14, 2016, the network did not display an on-screen logo in the bottom-right corner of the screen, except for a ten-second "Fox HD" promotional logo (until the end of 2010, which included a DirecTV sponsor tag); instead, a station logo bug was triggered in the right-hand corner of the 16:9 screen, disappearing during commercial breaks, even during local pre-emptions for breaking news or severe weather, though some stations like WGGB-DT2 in Springfield, Massachusetts, displayed only a "FOX" logo. Network or affiliate bugs are not shown during Fox Sports programming. During high-profile or live programs like American Idol and So You Think You Can Dance, Fox displays its network logo instead of the affiliate's for promotional reasons due to fair use of clips by other media. Until 2014, the bug was placed in the 4:3 safe area. Fox News Sunday displayed the "Fox HD" logo continuously due to both promotional and tape-delay reasons. On March 14, 2016, the standard Fox logo with hashtag was implemented across all programming, with the station bug flashing briefly at program start or after commercial breaks, as traditionally done by ABC, CBS, and NBC. The Fox HD bug was discontinued; it was still used on Fox News Sunday until late 2019–early 2020. On some Fox programs, a hashtag appears above the affiliate's logo (e.g., #newgirl or #bones) to provide viewers with program references.

During high-profile or live programs like American Idol and So You Think You Can Dance, Fox displayed its network logo instead of the affiliate's logo, primarily for promotional reasons due to fair use of clips by media outlets such as news programs, talk shows, and review or satirical content; until 2014, this bug was placed in the 4:3 safe area. Fox News Sunday displayed the "Fox HD" logo continuously due to both promotional reasons and because many stations aired the program on tape delay later in the morning. Beginning March 14, 2016, the standard Fox logo with hashtag was adopted for all programming, with the station bug flashed briefly at the start of a program or after commercial breaks, as traditionally done by ABC, CBS, and NBC stations; the Fox HD bug was discontinued, though it remained on Fox News Sunday until around late 2019–early 2020. On some Fox programs, a hashtag appears above the affiliate's logo (e.g., #newgirl or #bones) to link viewers to the network’s official Twitter search tag for discussions during broadcasts. In April 2012, episode-specific tags related to plot points (e.g., #saturdaynightGLEEver for a Glee episode) were introduced to generate trending topics and spread conversations on Twitter. When the Fox bug appears instead of the station logo, the Twitter hashtag is directly above the Fox logo in the safe area. Fox's World Series coverage began in HD with Game 1 of the 2002 World Series. During the analog-to-digital transition, Fox was the only U.S. commercial network to air widescreen programs not available in HD, labeled "Fox High Resolution Widescreen" from 2001 to 2006. Prior to its HD feed launch, some sitcoms and dramas aired in widescreen standard-definition, while reality, talk, and game shows (American Idol being the first major exception, starting in 2008) aired only in widescreen enhanced definition. This Week in Baseball began airing in widescreen in 2009, and Fox News Sunday transitioned to HD when the Fox News Channel moved to new high-definition facilities in November 2008; prior to the unified widescreen presentation on both HD and standard-definition feeds in September 2010, it was the last Fox News program to use 4:3 safe area graphics and camera positions. MADtv aired only in 4:3 until September 2008, likely due to tape-delaying by stations and producers not adopting the 16:9 format. The final Fox show to convert to HD was Family Guy, beginning with its September 26, 2010, episode; all programming is now broadcast in widescreen and high definition as of 2013, with Dolby Digital 5.1 surround sound. Fox is unique among American broadcasters in distributing its HD feed over satellite as an MPEG transport stream for bit-for-bit broadcast transmission; during network programming hours, local commercials are inserted using a transport stream splicer. Affiliates of other networks typically decode and re-encode compressed satellite feeds for over-the-air transmission. After Fox began broadcasting sports programming with 16:9-optimized graphics in late July 2010, it requested cable and satellite providers to use the No. 10 Active Format Description (AFD) flag, which displays 16:9 content in letterboxed format on 4:3 screens to ensure full display of graphical elements. Many Fox O&Os and affiliates began disseminating the AFD No. 10 flag for HD local news and syndicated programs, incorporating on-air graphics and logo bugs optimized for letterboxed presentation. In the early 1990s, Fox stations began using a branding structure combining "Fox" with the channel number and call letters (e.g., WNYW as "Fox 5"), later minimizing call letters to remain compliant with FCC rules, a trend followed by other networks. Branding varied by market: some stations used city or regional names (e.g., WFLD as "Fox Chicago" from 1997 to 2012, WTXF-TV as "Fox Philadelphia" from 1995 to 2003); others reduced "Fox" branding, using call letters or generic names (e.g., WSVN in Miami as "WSVN 7" and "(Channel) 7 News," KHON-TV in Honolulu changing from "Fox 2" to "KHON 2" in 2003, WDRB in Louisville dropping "Fox 41" to "WDRB" in 2011, KVRR in Fargo switching to "KVRR 15" in 2015). Stations that joined Fox through the 1994 New World deal retained Big Three-era branding (e.g., WJW in Cleveland dropped "TV8" and "Newscenter 8" for "Fox is ei8ht" and "ei8ht is News," KDFW in Dallas/Fort Worth rebranded to "Fox 4 Texas" and later to "Fox 4" with "Fox 4 News" since 1996). KTVU in Oakland-San Francisco retained "Channel 2" branding, rebranding to "KTVU Fox 2" in 1996 (adding the Fox logo beneath its "Circle Laser 2" logo), and adopting full-time "KTVU Fox 2" branding in February 2015, retaining the "Circle Laser 2" in both the standardized "boxkite" logo and an alternate version with a prominent Fox wordmark. KCPQ in Seattle retained "Q13 Fox" and "Q13 News" until September 2021, when it dropped "Q13" and rebranded to "Fox 13," aligning with other Fox O&Os. Starting in 2006, Fox O&Os adopted a standardized on-air look inspired by Fox News Channel, featuring a red, white, and blue boxkite logo with red pillars (rotating on-air, especially in logo bugs). After News Corporation acquired Myspace (sold in June 2011 to a group including Justin Timberlake), some O&Os launched websites with identical layouts and "MyFox" domains (e.g., MyFoxDC.com for WTTG). On-air use of the FNC-inspired logos declined in August 2012 with a new standardized graphics package using wordmark bugs; several O&Os discontinued "MyFox" domains by 2015. The use of Fox News Channel boxkite logos and connections to it was drastically reduced after Roger Ailes' July 2016 resignation, shifting to a simpler, more flexible "call-channel number" horizontal wordmark style suitable for traditional TV and mobile screens. In 2017, Stephen Arnold Music released a new news music package, "Beyond," which excluded all previous Fox News Channel sonic elements and was rolled out across all Fox O&O local news operations. As of 2017, Fox O&Os with sister MyNetworkTV stations began downplaying that network, with many adopting "Fox (channel number) Plus/Xtra/More" branding to suggest they are extensions of their sister Fox station, and many now carry extended newscasts or rebroadcasts of earlier newscasts during primetime, pushing MyNetworkTV’s schedule to late night. When Fox launched on October 9, 1986, as the Fox Broadcasting Company, it used a logo with three squares containing "FBC" similar to the UK’s BBC logo from 1997–present, with the network name in a rectangle below, mostly matching the color of ITV’s 1998–2004 logo, used primarily in the opening of The Late Show with Joan Rivers. On April 5, 1987, a more familiar logo based on 20th Century Fox’s design was introduced, featuring "FOX" with searchlights and a double-pane platform; Fox O&Os used a variant from 1987 to 1989 with an "O" and searchlight in negative space intersecting the "X" and panes; until the mid-1990s, some affiliates using CGI or local production houses emulated this design. In September 1993, the logo was modernized with a current proprietary logotype, angle changed (removing tilt), and the "O" gained a trademark pillar-like bowl, becoming a key element in advertising; the 1987 logo remained in print ads through 1993–94. Starting with this logo, Fox displayed an on-screen bug in the lower right corner (initially for one minute per segment, later throughout the program, then reverting after the 2009 digital transition). The "O" was later redesigned with the pillar, replacing the searchlight motif. A 1995–96 logo removed searchlights but kept two lower panes and added a third pane above the wordmark; a 1996 variant excluded the panes and restored searchlights behind the "F" and "X." The current logo, introduced in 1999, removed searchlights entirely and used only a wordmark. Despite this, searchlights remained part of 21st Century Fox branding, appearing in Fox News Channel’s logo and in the universal station logo introduced in 2006 by Fox O&Os (retained by seven former O&Os sold to Local TV in 2008 and spread to Tribune Broadcasting affiliates, modified in 2012 to feature one searchlight); the 1996–99 searchlight logo is still used by a few affiliates; searchlights were also in FX’s logo until 2008. The screen bug was used from 1999 to 2014; when the network upgraded to HD, the watermark remained in the 480i format. Until March 14, 2016, the network did not display the on-screen bug, only the hashtag without the Fox bug on some affiliates. For the 2019–20 season, Fox implemented branding by Trollbäck + Company, slightly thickening the logo and incorporating animations of its shapes into advertising and on-air elements, including an animation of abstract shapes morphing into the main Fox logo. Controversy arose in 2002 and 2003 over profanity by Cher and Nicole Richie during live broadcasts of the Billboard Music Awards on Fox affiliates in the Eastern and Central Time Zones, despite five-second audio delays; the indecent content was edited out in time zones west of the Mountain Time Zone. The Parents Television Council condemned both incidents as among the worst on television from 2001 to 2004 and filed tens of thousands of complaints with the FCC. Fox representatives’ apology was labeled a "sham" by PTC president L. Brent Bozell III, who argued the network could have easily used audio delays to remove the language. In 2004, Fox announced extending live delays to five minutes to allow easier editing of obscenities. In June 2007, the U.S. Second Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in Federal Communications Commission v. Fox Television Stations that the FCC could not fine broadcasters for fleeting expletives, such as during the Billboard Awards; the FCC later appealed the decision. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari and oral arguments began on November 4, 2008. The Parents Television Council has also criticized many popular Fox shows for perceived indecent content, including Family Guy, The Simpsons, American Dad!, Futurama, Cops, Hell's Kitchen, 24, House, Married... with Children, Bones, Arrested Development, Prison Break, 'Til Death, Malcolm in the Middle, The O.C., and That '70s Show, and has filed complaints with the FCC regarding such content.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) does not have the authority to fine broadcasters for fleeting expletives, as demonstrated in the case of the Billboard Awards. The FCC later decided to appeal the Second Circuit Court's decision. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari in FCC v. Fox, et al., and oral arguments began on November 4, 2008. The Parents Television Council has criticized numerous popular Fox shows for perceived indecent content, including Family Guy, The Simpsons, American Dad!, Futurama, Cops, Hell's Kitchen, 24, House, Married... with Children, Bones, Arrested Development, Prison Break, 'Til Death, Malcolm in the Middle, The O.C., and That '70s Show. The Council has filed complaints with the FCC regarding indecent content in these programs, specifically for That '70s Show and Married by America. The FCC successfully fined the network nearly $1 million for airing Married by America. This fine was reduced to $91,000 in January 2009 after Fox appealed, following the FCC's admission that it originally claimed to have received 159 complaints about the show, but later acknowledged receiving only 90—coming from just 23 individuals. A study by blogger Jeff Jarvis found that all but two of the complaints were nearly identical, indicating the $1.2 million judgment was based on original complaints from only three people. On September 21, 2012, the United States Department of Justice dismissed the lawsuit.
